prize_parts.citation: for visionary, densely patterned Romanian prose, rooted in poetry, in which memory, the body and dream are built into an expansive metaphysical project

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: Cărtărescu alone, one prize part. What has changed is how I would defend it. A convergence of preferences cannot count as a reason, and I have tried to test the case against the shared reservations and against Carson, my closest alternative. On the common criteria, Cărtărescu's case rests on a recognisable voice, formal control across very large structures (the Orbitor trilogy, published in English as Blinding, and Solenoid, as publicly described), and an imaginative and intellectual project that joins memory, the body and cosmology around a recurring set of images. The poetry is the formative ground of the prose, so the oeuvre has a visible line of development, though I can judge that line only partially. Carson's case is also serious. It rests on formal invention, depth in classical reception, and the recurring role of fragment and loss. I rank it second because the corpus is heterogeneous and a few celebrated hybrid works carry much of the argument. If the citation rested on her written lyric and essay work, I think that work could carry a case, but it would be a narrower claim than the one available for Cărtărescu. On citation scope, which the round 1 summary leaves open, I now prefer prose with poetry as its root. The wording says what the translated evidence best supports and still does not drop the poetry, and it avoids any regional or period label. All of this rests on public knowledge and the supplied descriptions. I have not independently verified any text.
statement.case_against: The reservation that decides how firmly I hold this is still translation. Much of what makes the prose distinctive is Romanian rhythm, syntax and sonic patterning. I can judge it only through translation, and the chair's summary shows that all six members are in the same position. The shared reservation is therefore a limit on all of us and not a point where we disagree. I also still cannot say whether the late novels' length is purposeful architecture or at times overextension. Claims that the repeated images prove structure, including my own in round 1, are inferences from public description and not demonstrated by close reading. I should treat them as hypotheses. Coverage of the early poetry and prose in translation is thin, so a whole-oeuvre citation is partly presumed. Against Carson, I have not resolved how much of her output counts as original literary authorship, given the translations and book-objects. Against my own preference, the near-unanimity of round 1 may mean the members have reasoned in parallel from the same thin evidence. It does not show that the case has been tested.

responses.point: Palm argues that the patterning is structural, with recurring images returning across volumes, and that the citation should name the project and not each book, so that it rests on the strongest sustained work and does not require every volume to be equal. She also says that if the committee judges by best individual books, Carson becomes a much closer comparison.
responses.response: I accept the second point and it affects my configuration. A citation that names the project and rests on the strongest sustained work is the right way to handle uneven volumes. But I would not use that move to avoid the question. Naming the project does not show that the project was sustained, and the pattern-versus-overextension test is still unanswered. On Carson, I take her point that the comparison depends on the standard applied: best individual books or sustained quality across a whole oeuvre. Under the first standard Carson is close. Under the second, which is the one in my protocol, I think Cărtărescu's case is better grounded, and the gap is smaller than my round 1 ranking suggested. That is why Carson stays as my first alternative.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg says the supplied evidence does not settle whether the late Cărtărescu novels extend the early project or repeat it. He would not treat length alone as a flaw, but he says it would be a serious objection if the late volumes repeated and did not extend.
responses.response: I take this as the sharpest statement of the open question, and I should correct my own round 1 wording. I wrote that the late novels extend the project in scale. That is the language of the shortlist description and of general public knowledge, not something I have tested. Extension in scale is also not the same as extension in vision. I would separate three things that the group has been running together: scale, recurrence and deepening. Scale is plain from the descriptions. Recurrence is plausible. Deepening is the claim that matters for maturity, and none of us can demonstrate it from translations. I keep my preference, but I hold the maturity claim as provisional on exactly the point Sem-Sandberg names.

responses.point: Carlberg argues that Carson's case depends on book-objects whose effect is partly material, and that the translations are a separate body of work, so a citation would have to decide how much of the oeuvre it covers. She finds the Cărtărescu citation easier to define because the achievement is carried by language.
responses.response: I agree that the scope problem is real and I have said so against my own first choice. I do not agree that it makes Carson's case merely harder to define. A citation resting on the original lyric, elegiac and essay work would be definable. It would just claim less. My difference with Carlberg is one of degree. I read the weight of the book-objects and translations as lowering Carson's ranking relative to Cărtărescu, not as removing her. I also accept her caution that the citation for Cărtărescu must not take a regional or postmodern frame. Her reading that his metaphysical architecture engages Nobel's 'idealistic tendency' more directly is, as she says, her own reading. I do not think the phrase separates the two candidates clearly, and I would not use it to decide between them.

responses.point: Sward says Carson's hybrid forms and Wright's reconstruction of the novel are also serious achievements, and that each is arguably less exposed to the translation problem in the form it takes in English. She would anchor the Cărtărescu citation in the prose and mention poetry cautiously.
responses.response: The first point has some force, but I would separate two things. A writer working in a language that members read directly gives us more confidence in our judgment. That concerns the committee's access, not the writer's merit, and the criteria are about the work. Still, access does affect how confident we can be, so I count it as an uncertainty about Cărtărescu and not as a point against him. On scope, I partly follow her. I prefer 'prose, rooted in poetry' to naming poetry as a co-equal part, because it matches what the translated evidence best supports and keeps the poetry in view. If a colleague who reads the Romanian poems can show that they stand independently, I would reconsider the wording.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's Romanian rhythm, syntax and sonic patterning survives in the English and French translations on which all six members' judgments rest. I cannot confirm this, and I know of no expert commentary on the Romanian original that I could rely on here.

Whether the late novels deepen the early project or partly repeat it. Scale and recurrence are visible from public description, but deepening is not demonstrated and needs close reading of the whole corpus.
Coverage of the early poetry and prose in translation is thin, so whether poetry is formative ground or an independent achievement cannot be settled for the citation wording.

For Carson, how far translations, book-objects and occasional pieces count as original authorship, and whether a citation resting on the written lyric and essay work would carry sustained quality across the oeuvre.
Whether the same view would hold under a best-individual-books standard instead of a whole-oeuvre standard. Palm suggests Carson would then be much closer, and I think that is plausible.

My assessments rest on public knowledge and the supplied descriptions. I have not independently verified any source. The votes of the six members are a modelling assumption, including the co-opted member's, and the full Swedish Academy makes any actual award decision.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. The profile documents no personal, professional or institutional relationship with any shortlisted writer, and no recusal is warranted on that record. My scholarly interests in the literary fragment, exile literature and the translation of Celan overlap thematically with Carson's use of fragment and translation and, more loosely, with Zurita's poetic sequences. I list both as alternatives, so I disclose this overlap. It is context only and not evidence of preference. I am also chair and wrote the round 1 summary, so my own positions are among those it records. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
